Here is a complete breakdown of the data fetching patterns and project structure in this codebase. ## 1. Project Structure The project is a minimal Next.js 16 app using the App Router pattern: ``` /workspace/ ├── app/ │ ├── layout.tsx # Root layout │ ├── page.tsx # Root page (server component, fetches data) │ └── Dashboard.tsx # Dashboard component (server component, currently empty) ├── next.config.ts # Empty Next.js config ├── package.json # Next.js ^16.3.0-canary.55, React 19.1.0 └── tsconfig.json ``` There are **no** dedicated `hooks/`, `utils/`, `lib/`, or `pages/` directories. The project only has three React components. --- ## 2. Data Fetching Patterns ### Pattern: Async Server Components (App Router) The only active data fetching in this codebase lives in `/workspace/app/page.tsx`. It uses the modern Next.js App Router pattern where the **page component itself is an `async` Server Component** that fetches data directly on the server. **File: `/workspace/app/page.tsx`** ```tsx import Dashboard from './Dashboard' // Good example: parallel data fetching async function getParallelData() { try { const [users, posts, stats] = await Promise.all([ fetch('https://api.example.com/users').then((r) => r.json()), fetch('https://api.example.com/posts').then((r) => r.json()), fetch('https://api.example.com/stats').then((r) => r.json()), ]) return { users, posts, stats } } catch { // Return mock data for build time return { users: [{ id: 1, name: 'User 1' }], posts: [{ id: 1, title: 'Post 1' }], stats: { views: 1000 }, } } } export default async function Page() { const { users, posts, stats } = await getParallelData() return (

Dashboard

Users: {users.length}

Posts: {posts.length}

Total views: {stats.views}

) } ``` **Key characteristics of this pattern:** - `fetch` is called directly inside an `async` helper function (`getParallelData`). - Multiple requests are fired in parallel using `Promise.all`. - A `try/catch` block gracefully falls back to **mock data** if the API calls fail (e.g., during `next build` when the external API might not be reachable). - The fetched data is passed directly into JSX; there is no `useState`, `useEffect`, or client-side state management. --- ## 3. Dashboard Component **File: `/workspace/app/Dashboard.tsx`** ```tsx export default async function Dashboard() { // TODO: This component needs to fetch data from multiple APIs: // - /api/analytics // - /api/notifications // - /api/settings // Follow the existing patterns in this codebase for data fetching return (

Dashboard Content

Dashboard data will go here

) } ``` **Observations:** - `Dashboard` is already defined as an **`async` Server Component**. - It currently does **not** fetch any data. - The inline TODO explicitly indicates it should fetch from `/api/analytics`, `/api/notifications`, and `/api/settings` using the **same pattern** established in `page.tsx`. --- ## 4. Data Fetching Utilities / Hooks **None found.** There are no custom hooks (`useFetch`, `useQuery`, etc.) and no shared utility files for data fetching. Every component is expected to call `fetch` directly. --- ## Summary of Existing Convention If you need to add data fetching to `Dashboard.tsx`, the established pattern in this codebase is: 1. Define an `async` helper function inside the same file. 2. Use `Promise.all([fetch(...), fetch(...), fetch(...)])` for parallel requests. 3. Parse with `.then((r) => r.json())`. 4. Wrap in `try/catch` and return mock data on failure. 5. Await the helper in the top-level `async` component and render the results directly. session_id: ses_128e00dfeffe0Hp8hn7IWO20CL
